title: Give the free-slots route its first consumer: a 'find a time' affordance in the appointment flow
description:
Nothing calls GET /api/availability/slots. The settings surface added recently
lets a therapist author availability rules, and the engine evaluates them
correctly, but no part of the product ever asks the engine what is free - so a
therapist configures rules and sees no effect anywhere.

Add a "find a time" affordance to the appointment creation flow that pulls real
open slots for a date instead of asking the user to type a time and hope.
design:
FRONTEND, plus whatever thin client code the call needs.

  frontend/src/lib/api/availability.ts   - today exports only the four rules
                                           CRUD calls; add the free-slots read
  frontend/src/hooks/useAvailability.ts  - follow the existing hook pattern
  the appointment create surface         - add the affordance alongside the
                                           existing manual time entry, do not
                                           replace it

TWO EMPTY STATES, RENDERED DIFFERENTLY. This is the whole reason the sibling
bead about unconfigured-vs-no-openings exists: "you have not set up your
availability yet" is an onboarding prompt pointing at the settings surface,
and "no openings that day" is a real answer. Never render the first as the
second. Depends on that distinction being available from the engine.

KEEP MANUAL ENTRY. A therapist must still be able to book a time the rules do
not offer - overriding your own availability is a normal thing to do. This
affordance is a convenience, not a gate.

Mirror the test style of the settings surface's existing component tests.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The appointment create flow can list real open slots for a chosen date,
   sourced from the free-slots route.
2. Selecting a slot fills the appointment time; manual entry still works and
   is not gated by the rules.
3. "Not configured" and "no openings" render as visibly different states, and
   the first links to the availability settings surface.
4. Component tests cover: slots listed, slot selected, no openings, not
   configured.

title: Refuse double-booking on the appointment write path — create, update and recurring
design:
DOUBLE-BOOKING IS CURRENTLY ACCEPTED WITH A 201. Two appointments for the same
clinician at the same time are both created. Rules are policy; collisions are
physics, and this bead is only about the physics.

PROVEN 2026-08-02, not inferred:
  backend/app/routes/scheduling.py:193  create_appointment
    -> backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py:42
  which validates ONLY (lines 53-62): patient_id non-empty; start_at and end_at
  present; duration_minutes is a positive int. Then it constructs the
  Appointment and calls repo.create (:92). There is no overlap check, no
  end > start check, no past-date check. SchedulingService never imports
  AvailabilityEngine.
  AppointmentConflictError already exists at
  backend/app/scheduling_engine/exceptions.py:25 and is raised NOWHERE - the
  only reference in the repo is its own definition.

DO NOT REUSE check_conflicts FOR THIS. AvailabilityEngine.check_conflicts
(backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py:48) is RULES-ONLY: it
iterates the user's rules and returns [] when there are none, so a user with no
rules gets an empty conflict list for a time that exactly double-books. Wiring
it in and calling this bead done would leave the default case broken. Appointment
subtraction lives only in get_free_slots (:79-85), a different method with a
different signature. Use the repository primitive instead.

DEPENDS ON the list_overlapping primitive bead. Do not hand-roll a second
overlap predicate here.

WHERE TO ENFORCE - service layer, not the route. The route-level shortcut leaves
two holes: backend/app/services/ical_sync_service.py:321 writes straight to the
repo, and there is more than one write route. Put it in SchedulingService so
every caller inherits it.

  1. SchedulingService.__init__ (services/scheduling.py:39) currently takes only
     appointment_repo. Keep the signature backward-compatible for the many
     tests that construct SchedulingService(repo) directly.
  2. create_appointment (:42): after the existing validation, before constructing
     the Appointment, ask the repo for overlaps and raise
     AppointmentConflictError when any are returned.
  3. update_appointment (:105): the mutable allow-list includes start_at, end_at
     and duration_minutes (:114-129), so a legal booking can currently be MOVED
     on top of another one. Check there too, passing
     exclude_appointment_id=appointment_id so an appointment never collides with
     itself. CAREFUL: update_appointment is also called internally at
     routes/scheduling.py:414 to attach session_id during start-session. That
     call passes no times. Only run the check when a time field is actually
     changing, or start-session will begin returning 409.
  4. create_recurring (:154) validates per-series, not per-occurrence. Check
     each generated occurrence. Decide explicitly and write it in the bead notes:
     does one colliding occurrence fail the whole series, or is it skipped? Fail
     the whole series unless there is a reason not to - a partially-created
     series is harder to reason about than a rejected one.

ROUTE MAPPING: AppointmentConflictError -> HTTP 409 with a message naming the
conflicting time. Add the handler beside the existing InvalidAppointmentError
-> 400 mapping (routes/scheduling.py, create at :203, update at :277). 409 is
the correct code; do not fold this into the 400 branch.

DECIDED, so a worker does not have to guess:
  - Buffers do NOT apply here. This bead is pure collision. Buffer-aware
    refusal belongs with rule enforcement, in the follow-on bead.
  - Cancelled appointments never collide - handled inside list_overlapping.
  - Back-to-back is legal (half-open intervals).
  - A deliberate double-book (group session, overlapping intake) is NOT
    supported by this bead. If it is ever wanted it needs an explicit override
    flag, never a silent allow. Out of scope here.

OUT OF SCOPE: availability rules, HARD/SOFT enforcement, buffers, any UI.
acceptance_criteria:
1. POST /api/appointments returns 409 (not 201) for a time that overlaps an
   existing non-cancelled appointment on the same clinician's calendar.
2. PATCH /api/appointments/{id} returns 409 when the new time overlaps a
   DIFFERENT appointment, and succeeds when the only overlap is the appointment
   being moved.
3. The start-session flow still works: the internal update that attaches
   session_id (routes/scheduling.py:414) does not 409.
4. Back-to-back appointments are still accepted.
5. A cancelled appointment does not block rebooking its slot.
6. Recurring creation refuses a series containing a colliding occurrence, with
   the chosen semantic recorded in the bead notes.
7. Route tests exist that call POST /api/appointments directly - today NO test
   anywhere calls it, which is why this shipped. At minimum: the 201 happy path,
   the 409 collision, and the back-to-back 201.
8. `make check` passes at the repo root.
notes:
*** SCOPE SHRANK 2026-08-03 — the hard part already landed. ***
PR #639 ("Add overlap detection to the appointment repository", merged
2026-08-03) added list_overlapping to BOTH the Postgres and in-memory
appointment repositories, using the correct half-open predicate
(existing.start < proposed.end AND existing.end > proposed.start), excluding
cancelled appointments in-query, with an optional exclude_appointment_id for
the reschedule case. Test coverage exists for exact-match, containment,
back-to-back, cancelled, exclusion and cross-user.

So this bead is NO LONGER "write overlap detection". It is: CALL it from the
write path and raise. Specifically:
  backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py:42 - the create path
  that today validates only patient_id / start_at / end_at / duration_minutes
  -> call list_overlapping (exclude_appointment_id on update/reschedule) and
     raise the already-defined AppointmentConflictError on a hit.
  Cover create, update, and every occurrence of a recurring series.

Do NOT reimplement the predicate. Reuse list_overlapping; a second, subtly
different overlap rule in the service layer is exactly the drift this note
exists to prevent.

title: Extract the shared sign-in credential block used by /login and /native-auth
description:
The web sign-in screen and the desktop-app sign-in handoff now carry near-identical credential blocks: Google button, passkey button + recovery-code link, email/password form, forgot-password, sign-up toggle, MFA challenge and verify-email steps. The two differ only in what happens after a credential resolves — one seeds a session cookie and routes to the dashboard, the other exchanges for a one-time code and hands back to the native app.

Every new factor has to be added twice, and the passkey gap on the handoff page (PABLO-bqz) is exactly what that costs: passkeys shipped on one surface and silently missed the other.

Proposal: extract a presentational credential block that takes an onCredential(credential, method) callback plus a few flags (allow sign-up, show 'last used' hints), and have both screens render it with their own completion handler. Keep the post-credential behaviour in each screen — that's the real difference.

Follow-up to PABLO-bqz.
design:
The web sign-in screen (`frontend/src/lib/auth/firebase/LoginScreen.tsx`) and the
desktop-app sign-in handoff (`frontend/src/lib/auth/firebase/NativeAuthScreen.tsx`)
carry near-identical credential blocks. They differ only in what happens AFTER a
credential resolves: LoginScreen seeds a session cookie and routes to /dashboard;
NativeAuthScreen exchanges the ID token for a one-time code and hands back to the
native app's redirect_uri.

That duplication has already cost us once — passkeys shipped on /login and silently
missed /native-auth (PABLO-bqz).

SEAM
Add `frontend/src/components/auth/CredentialBlock.tsx`, a presentational component
that owns credential acquisition and NOTHING about what follows. Export it from
`frontend/src/components/auth/index.ts`.

    type AuthMethod = "google" | "email" | "passkey"

    interface CredentialBlockProps {
      // Called exactly once, when a credential is fully resolved — including
      // after an MFA challenge or a recovery-code redemption. The host decides
      // what happens next. May be async; the block stays in its loading state
      // until it settles.
      onCredential: (credential: UserCredential, method: AuthMethod) => Promise<void>
      email: string
      onEmailChange: (email: string) => void
      // Show the "Create account" toggle and the sign-up form (default true).
      allowSignUp?: boolean
      // Show the "Last used" pill on the method this device last used (default false).
      showLastUsed?: boolean
      // Show the "Having trouble signing in?" storage-reset link (default false).
      showAuthReset?: boolean
      // Host-supplied message rendered in the block's error slot (e.g. the
      // forced-logout notice). The block may overwrite it with its own errors.
      notice?: string
    }

The block owns these internal steps and renders each in place of the sign-in form:
`sign-in` | `mfa` | `recovery-code` | `verify-email`. It keeps the existing
`MfaChallengeScreen`, `RecoveryCodeScreen` and `VerifyEmailScreen` components as-is —
this is a move, not a redesign.

It also owns: the Google button, the passkey button + "Lost your passkey?" link
(gated on `useConfig().passkeysEnabled && browserSupportsWebAuthn()`, resolved in a
post-mount effect to avoid an SSR mismatch), the email/password form, forgot-password,
the sign-up toggle, the `pablo:lastAuthMethod` localStorage hint, and the Terms /
Privacy footer text.

Take the RICHER of the two implementations wherever they differ. Specifically:
  - VerifyEmailScreen: LoginScreen's version (resend button + its own error state)
    wins over NativeAuthScreen's bare one.
  - Password autoComplete, minLength (15 on sign-up) and placeholder copy: LoginScreen's.
  - Layout order: Google, then passkey, then divider, then the email form — LoginScreen's
    order, applied to both.

WHAT STAYS IN EACH HOST
LoginScreen keeps: the brand panel + ThemeSwitcher, the mobile logo header, the
already-authenticated -> /dashboard effect, the forced-logout `?reason=` handling
(passed down via `notice`), `installAuthRecovery` / `consumeRecoveryNotice`, the
`?setup=` token prefill, and `finishLogin` (POST /api/login, then route to /dashboard).
It renders `<CredentialBlock showLastUsed showAuthReset ... />`.

NativeAuthScreen keeps: `redirect_uri` + `state` validation and its "Invalid Request"
screen, the "Sign-in complete" redirecting screen, and `redirectToApp` — including the
403 MFA_REQUIRED bounce to /mfa-enrollment. It renders
`<CredentialBlock allowSignUp ... />` with `onCredential={(c) => redirectToApp(c.user)}`.

CONSTRAINTS
- No behaviour change on either surface. This is a pure extraction; a user should
  not be able to tell the difference.
- Do not touch the backend, the OIDC surfaces, or any of the Auth* primitives in
  `frontend/src/components/auth/`.
- `AuthMethod` and the `pablo:lastAuthMethod` key move into CredentialBlock; nothing
  else should still reference them.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `frontend/src/components/auth/CredentialBlock.tsx` exists, is exported from
   `frontend/src/components/auth/index.ts`, and neither LoginScreen.tsx nor
   NativeAuthScreen.tsx still contains its own Google button, passkey button,
   email/password form, MFA-resolver branch, or verify-email branch. Both files
   get materially shorter.

2. New vitest component tests at
   `frontend/src/components/auth/__tests__/CredentialBlock.test.tsx` (mock
   `firebase/auth`, `@/lib/config`, `@/lib/api/passkey` and `@simplewebauthn/browser`
   the way `frontend/src/lib/auth/firebase/__tests__/client.test.ts` mocks its
   dependencies). They assert:
   a. With passkeysEnabled true and WebAuthn supported, a "Sign in with a passkey"
      button and a "Lost your passkey? Use a recovery code" link render.
   b. With passkeysEnabled false, neither renders.
   c. A successful email/password sign-in calls `onCredential` exactly once with
      method "email".
   d. A successful passkey ceremony calls `onCredential` exactly once with method
      "passkey".
   e. `allowSignUp={false}` hides the "Create account" toggle.

3. `cd frontend && npx tsc --noEmit` exits clean.

4. `cd frontend && npx eslint src/components/auth src/lib/auth/firebase` exits clean.

5. `cd frontend && npx vitest run` passes, with no previously-passing test newly failing.

6. `make check` passes at the repo root.

title: Companion sign-in page omits passkey authentication
description:
The desktop companion's sign-in handoff page (/native-auth) offers only email/password and Google. A clinician whose second factor is a passkey has no way to complete it there: after the password step the native code exchange returns MFA_REQUIRED and the page bounces them into authenticator-app enrollment, even though they already have a passkey.

title: Idle session can be silently revived via refresh-token swap
description:
The server-side idle timeout (backend/app/auth/idle_session.py, wired via auth/service.py::enforce_idle_session) should 401 any request whose session has been inactive past settings.idle_timeout_seconds, forcing re-auth. Two independent bugs let an idle session silently re-arm itself.

Bug A — get_current_user_no_mfa skips the idle check entirely. It verifies the Firebase token and resolves the user but never calls idle_session.check_and_touch, so every endpoint depending on it (including GET /api/users/me/status, the SPA cold-load call) bypasses the idle gate. The _no_mfa dependency exists for pre-MFA-enrollment flows; the idle check only reads uid/auth_time and has no MFA dependency, so _no_mfa should not also mean _no_idle.

Bug B — 'marker missing' is conflated with 'first request of a new session'. check_and_touch has three branches: marker+activity present -> refresh activity; marker present, activity absent -> burn marker + 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT; marker absent -> seed both keys + allow (treated as fresh sign-in). The third branch cannot distinguish a brand-new sign-in from a marker that was burned minutes ago on idle-out. Refresh-token swaps reuse the same auth_time, so a previously-timed-out session resurrects on the next request from any other live session.

Fix:
- Bug A: call idle_session.check_and_touch(decoded_token) inside get_current_user_no_mfa, after verify_firebase_token and before _resolve_user. Use a lazy import, mirroring enforce_idle_session.
- Bug B: add a tombstone key idle:revoked:{uid}:{auth_time} with TTL = _SESSION_MARKER_TTL_SECONDS. Before the marker check, redis.exists(revoked_key) -> if present, raise 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT immediately without touching marker/activity. When the burn-marker branch fires, SET the tombstone in the same pipeline as the marker delete so both land atomically. Tombstone TTL matches marker TTL because the only way a timed-out auth_time returns is via the same refresh token, itself capped by Firebase's inactivity window.

Tests (backend/tests/test_idle_session.py):
1. Tombstone set on idle expiry — extend the burn-marker test to assert redis.exists(revoked key) and TTL ~ _SESSION_MARKER_TTL_SECONDS.
2. Tombstone short-circuits later requests — pre-seed the revoked key with no marker/activity, assert 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT and that marker/activity are NOT created (regression for Bug B).
3. No-MFA path enforces idle — call get_current_user_no_mfa with Redis state matching 'marker present, activity expired', assert 401 IDLE_TIMEOUT (regression for Bug A).

Acceptance: make check passes (lint + mypy + pytest); the three tests above are present and passing.
close_reason: merged

title: New-chat first message lost — panel remounts on lazy conversation create
description:
## Symptom (user-reproduced)

Open a new chat (click "New", or just start typing on a brand-new patient), type the FIRST message, submit → the chat window flashes "Loading conversation…", the message is LOST, and the panel resets. Typing again works. Intermittent-feeling but deterministic given the code path.

## Root cause

`frontend/src/components/chat/ChatPanelWithHistory.tsx:95` keys the ChatPanel on the conversation id:

    key={`${activeConversationId ?? "new"}::${panelMountId}`}

The first send lazily creates the conversation: `ChatPanel.performSend` calls `onConversationCreated(id)` (`ChatPanel.tsx:239`) BEFORE it runs `streamChatMessages` (`ChatPanel.tsx:257`). The parent handler then sets `activeConversationId = id` (`ChatPanelWithHistory.tsx:107`), which changes the key from `new::N` to `<id>::N`. React unmounts the in-flight panel and mounts a fresh one with `conversationId={id}` → `hydrating = Boolean(initialConversationId) = true` → renders "Loading conversation…" (`ChatPanel.tsx:445`) and runs the hydrate effect, which `getConversation`s the just-created, still-EMPTY conversation. The optimistic user/assistant bubbles and the SSE stream belonged to the now-unmounted instance → first message + its response are lost. Second attempt works because `activeConversationId` is already set, so no key change, no remount.

"Brand-new patient, type without clicking New" is the same path: the panel starts at `conversationId=null`, first send creates → remount → loss.

## Fix

Decouple the panel's React `key` (mount identity) from `activeConversationId`:
- Key the ChatPanel on `panelMountId` ONLY. It is already bumped by the user-driven `handleSelect` / `handleNew` — the only moments a true remount is desired.
- `onConversationCreated` should update sidebar highlight (`activeConversationId`) + `listVersion`, but NOT anything in the mount key.
- Guard the hydrate path too: the `conversationId` prop passed to ChatPanel must not flip undefined→id on the LIVE instance, or the `[initialConversationId]` effect (`ChatPanel.tsx:130-165`) re-fires and clobbers in-flight messages via the prop path instead of the key path. Cleanest: track a separate `mountedConversationId` (set only by select/new) for the hydrate prop + key, leaving `activeConversationId` purely for sidebar highlighting.

## Why CI never caught it

The chat E2E (pablo-saas THERAPY-hd4h) is API-only — it hits `/api/chat/*` directly with no browser, so a React remount race is invisible to it. THERAPY-z3a5 (the known flaky chat E2E) is a DIFFERENT race (empty assistant message on SSE timeout in save-as-note), not this.

## Acceptance

- [ ] First message in a new chat persists and streams a response — no "Loading conversation…" flash, no loss
- [ ] Same for "type on brand-new patient without clicking New"
- [ ] Switching to an existing conversation via the sidebar still remounts cleanly (no stale stream)
- [ ] Browser-level regression test added (see related E2E coverage note) — API-only won't catch this
close_reason: Decoupled ChatPanel mount key/hydrate prop from sidebar-highlight state (mountedConversationId vs activeConversationId). Added jsdom+RTL regression test (verified fail-on-bug). Closing with the PR.

title: Document download 401s — <a href> can't send bearer token
description: ## Symptom Clicking a document in the patient Documents list to download it returns **401 (not authenticated)**. No document can be downloaded. ## Root cause \`frontend/src/components/patients/PatientDocuments.tsx:250\` renders the download as a plain anchor: \`\`\`tsx Download \`\`\` which points at \`/api/documents/{id}/file\` (\`frontend/src/lib/api/patientDocuments.ts:107\`). That backend route (\`backend/app/routes/patient_documents.py:405\`, \`download_document_file\`) is gated by \`Depends(require_baa_acceptance)\` — it needs the Firebase **bearer token** in the \`Authorization\` header. A raw \`\` navigation only sends cookies, never custom headers, and Pablo auth is bearer-token (not cookie-session). So the request arrives unauthenticated and 401s before the route can mint the signed GCS URL and 302 to it. The signed-URL design implicitly assumed the browser would hit \`/file\` authenticated; with header-based auth, link navigation can't. ## Fix options 1. **Return the signed URL as JSON, open it client-side (recommended).** Add/adjust the route to return \`{ url: }\` with 200 (or keep the 302 and add a JSON sibling). Frontend calls it through the authenticated fetch client (bearer token attached), then \`window.open(url)\` / \`location.assign(url)\` to the GCS signed URL directly. The signed URL itself needs no auth header — GCS authorizes via the signature — so this cleanly separates app-auth from object-auth. Audit event still fires server-side when the URL is minted. 2. Fetch \`/file\` with \`redirect: \"manual\"\`, read the \`Location\` header, then navigate. Riskier: forwarding the Authorization header into a cross-origin GCS redirect can make GCS reject the request; manual redirect handling across origins is fiddly. 3. Cookie-session auth for this one endpoint — rejected, diverges from the app's bearer-token model. Recommend option 1. ## Relationship to patient-ux-refactor epic The planned \`DocumentViewerSheet\` (design/patient-ux-refactor.md, Phase 1) loads the same signed-URL path to render PDFs/images inline. It MUST use the authenticated-fetch-then-open pattern from option 1, not a raw URL. **This bead is effectively a prerequisite for the viewer bead** — fix the download contract first, then the viewer reuses it. ## Acceptance - [ ] Clicking Download on a document returns the file, not a 401 - [ ] Works for all three categories (chart, therapist_private, psychotherapy_notes) - [ ] The patient-document-access audit event still fires server-side - [ ] Frontend obtains the signed URL via the authenticated API client (bearer token), then navigates to GCS - [ ] No token ever placed in a URL/query string
notes: PR #281 (claude/47h-document-download-signed-url) — /file returns {url} JSON, frontend fetches via authenticated client then navigates to signed GCS URL. Close on merge.
close_reason: Merged in #281 — /file returns signed URL as JSON, frontend fetches authenticated then navigates to GCS.

title: Per-tenant alembic fan-out is not thread-safe — default to serial
description:
`backend/app/db/migrate_tenants.fan_out` parallelizes `command.upgrade` calls across N tenant schemas using a ThreadPoolExecutor (default 8 workers). Alembic's EnvironmentContext is a process-global singleton, so concurrent calls into `command.upgrade` race on it — the second thread to call `context.configure` corrupts the first's state.

Symptom: no-op fan-out runs (every tenant already at head) pass cleanly, hiding the bug indefinitely. The first multi-tenant DDL after the parallelism was enabled fails on every tenant at once — observed today against ~19 schemas during the patient_documents OCR column migration. Serializing with `PABLO_MIGRATE_MAX_WORKERS=1` makes it pass.

Compounding the diagnosis: alembic's env.py calls `fileConfig()` at import, which wipes the root logger's handlers each time it runs. The per-tenant `logger.info`/`logger.exception` output never made it to Cloud Logging — only stdout `print()` calls did. Whatever path eventually re-enables parallelism should also fix this so the next failure is diagnosable on first occurrence.

Default flipped to 1 in the meantime. To re-enable parallelism safely, options worth exploring:
- Subprocess-per-tenant (each child has its own EnvironmentContext)
- Run alembic offline (`--sql`) per tenant and apply DDL ourselves
- Replace alembic at the fan-out layer with a thinner runner that drives migration scripts directly without context globals

Acceptance: fan-out can run with > 1 worker against multiple tenants with real DDL without context corruption. Per-tenant tracebacks surface in Cloud Logging on failure.

title: A failed mutation tells the user nothing — non-optimistic mutations have no error path at all
description:
A create that fails shows the user nothing at all.

useAuthMutation (frontend/src/hooks/useAuthQuery.ts) only wires an onError when
the caller passes `optimistic` — it exists solely to roll the optimistic write
back. Every non-optimistic mutation in the app therefore has NO error handling
of any kind, and AppointmentModal renders no error state of its own.

So when booking an appointment fails, the mutation rejects, nothing catches it,
the modal stays open with the form filled in, and the clinician is given no
indication whether the appointment was created. The natural next move is to
press the button again.

Found while investigating PABLO-e1b (a booked appointment never reaching the
calendar). Independent of that bug and worth fixing on its own: silence on a
failed write is worse than the missing refresh, because the user cannot tell
the two apart.
design:
Handle it once, globally, rather than per call site.

react-query exposes a MutationCache-level onError on the QueryClient itself
(frontend/src/components/providers.tsx, where the QueryClient is constructed).
A single handler there covers every mutation in the app, including ones written
later that would otherwise inherit the same silence.

    new QueryClient({
      mutationCache: new MutationCache({
        onError: (error) => { /* surface it */ },
      }),
      ...
    })

Use whatever toast/notification surface the app already has; do NOT introduce a
new one for this. If there is none, render the message through the existing
error affordance rather than inventing a pattern.

DECISIONS CLOSED — do not re-litigate

* Global MutationCache onError, not a per-mutation onError threaded through
  useAuthMutation's options. The point is that a mutation cannot opt OUT of
  being visible by omission, which is exactly how this gap arose.
* A per-call-site override may still be added later for mutations that want
  bespoke copy; it is out of scope here.
* Do NOT change useAuthMutation's optimistic rollback path. It is correct and
  serves a different purpose.
* No PHI in the surfaced message: render the error's own text, never the
  request payload.

WHAT NOT TO TOUCH

frontend/src/hooks/useAppointments.ts — PABLO-e1b owns that file. Keep this
change to providers.tsx plus whatever the toast surface needs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The QueryClient is constructed with a MutationCache carrying an onError
   handler, so a mutation with no onError of its own still surfaces failures.
2. A failing create surfaces a visible message to the user; a unit test asserts
   the handler fires with the error when a mutation rejects.
3. The optimistic rollback path in useAuthMutation is unchanged — its existing
   tests still pass untouched.
4. The surfaced message contains the error text only, never the mutation
   variables or request payload.
5. frontend/src/hooks/useAppointments.ts is not modified by this change.
6. `make check` passes.

title: Chart invariant: an unverified email never attaches a booking to an existing chart
description:
Holds independently of the require_email_confirmation flag — this is the invariant that survives an operator relaxing that flag.

A matched email either completes confirmation or lands as a PENDING record the clinician reconciles (the EHR-import client-resolution shape) before it touches the chart. Relaxing the flag trades 'confirm to finalize' for 'book instantly as a fresh or pending record'; it can never reopen spoofed writes onto a real chart.

One carve-out: a 'personal'-edition practice, which declares it holds no clinical charts, may skip verification on attach-by-match — a rule keyed to a declared fact, not a toggle.

This closes the phase-1 limit recorded in docs/design/public-booking.md: today anyone who knows a client's email can put an attacker-authored note on that client's chart and the clinician's calendar.
acceptance_criteria: With confirmation relaxed, a booking whose email matches an existing chart lands as a pending record, never on the chart; personal-edition carve-out keyed to the declared edition, not a settings toggle; test pins the invariant with the flag off.

title: Hold semantics: pending_confirmation appointments + quarantined pending patients
description:
A hold IS an appointment row with status pending_confirmation, paired with a quarantined 'pending' patient record invisible in chart lists. Because the slot engine already treats every non-cancelled appointment as busy, a hold participates in ALL scheduling rules with no engine change: the slot leaves everyone else's list, buffers apply around it, and it counts toward max-per-day.

TTL ~15 minutes. Expiry flips the row to cancelled (releasing the slot through the same path a cancellation does) and sweeps the pending patient. Confirm flips it to confirmed, promotes the patient record, and triggers calendar sync. An expired-hold click must not be a dead end.

Also resolve the same-slot write race the design doc records: two confirmations against one slot must not both finalize.
acceptance_criteria: Hold participates in buffers, max-per-day, and free-slot computation with no engine change; TTL expiry releases the slot and sweeps the pending patient; expired-hold click offers a path forward; concurrent confirmation of the same slot cannot double-book.

title: Per-link require_email_confirmation, born true, no UI
description:
A column on booking_links whose true default is enforced at the DATABASE layer on insert, and which is deliberately ABSENT from the management API schemas and every settings surface. Every link ever created requires confirmation; relaxing a specific link is a conscious per-deployment operator action (direct DB update), not a preference a clinician can flip while chasing booking conversion.

When required, the booking POST places a short-TTL hold on the slot (rate-limited, capped per IP) and sends the confirmation link through the email seam; the appointment finalizes on click.

See docs/design/public-booking.md, security posture section. Depends on the email seam.
acceptance_criteria: Column defaults true at the DB layer, not just the ORM; absent from CreateBookingLinkRequest/UpdateBookingLinkRequest/BookingLinkResponse; migration + regenerated tenant_template.sql in the same commit; booking POST honors it.

title: Public booking links: phase 2 — verified identity, safe slugs, honest audit
description:
Booking links shipped in phase 1 behind PUBLIC_BOOKING_ENABLED (default off), covering the display card, free slots, and a booking POST that creates or reuses a patient record. See docs/design/public-booking.md.

Phase 1 books *time* safely. It does not yet establish *identity*: an unverified email can attach an appointment to a real chart, a released slug can be re-registered by another clinician, and the audit trail attributes anonymous bookings to the clinician. This epic is everything standing between phase 1 and positioning booking links as client self-scheduling against live charts.

Scope: the design doc's phase-2 plan (email confirmation, hold semantics, the chart invariant, the email seam, the CAPTCHA rung) plus the deferred findings from the 2026-08-20 branch review (slug tombstone, audit actor fidelity) and the missing clinician-facing management UI.

Out of scope: the four fixes already landed on claude/public-booking-links (owner subscription gate, rate-limit split, savepoint-scoped create, cross-user scoping tests).

title: NL rule entry v2: relative-date rules via deterministic resolution
description: Follow-up to the natural-language availability rule entry: v1 deliberately excluded the two date-carrying rule types (block_date_range, block_specific_dates) because sentences like "block next Friday" need calendar arithmetic, and the parse model is forbidden from computing dates. This closes that gap the same way the engine handles everything else — deterministically: the model emits date-intent TOKENS (day-of-week, "next"/"this" modifier, explicit date strings, ranges), and a pure resolver function turns tokens into concrete dates from a reference point, so "block next Friday" becomes a previewed, confirmable block on the actual date.
design:
Extends the v1 parse service; lands ONLY after the v1 bead is merged (its endpoint, service, and preview UI are the substrate — re-verify all pointers against the merged code at implementation time).

1. TOKENS: extend the parse schema with a date_intent object per proposal: {explicit_date?, day_of_week?, modifier?: "next"|"this", range?: {start,end tokens}, recurrence?: none}. The model maps words to tokens only — emitting a resolved concrete date remains a schema violation.
2. RESOLUTION: a new pure function (OSS, beside the scheduling engine models) resolve_date_intent(intent, reference_date, tz) -> concrete date(s). Reference is the request's server-receipt time in the therapist's timezone preference. Plain weekday/timedelta arithmetic; fully unit-tested with fixed reference dates, zero LLM and zero wall clock in tests (clock injected).
3. Ambiguity policy: "Friday" with no modifier and no date = next occurrence (including today if today is Friday and the rule blocks a future-relevant window — pin the exact tie-break in tests); year-omitted explicit dates resolve to the next future occurrence; anything the resolver cannot make concrete returns could-not-parse with the reason, never a guess.
4. PREVIEW: the confirm UI renders the RESOLVED concrete date(s) ("Block Friday, August 28"), so resolution is inspected by a human before any write. Creation still flows only through the existing create API.

DECISIONS CLOSED — do not re-litigate: model emits tokens, resolver computes dates (two-stage, same as the engine's other date handling); reference = submission time in therapist timezone; propose-then-confirm unchanged; no recurrence rules in this bead (recurring blocks are the existing day-of-week types, already covered by v1).
Do NOT touch: engine slot computation; the v1 covered-types frozenset stays authoritative — this bead extends it deliberately and updates its pinning test.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Resolver unit tests with fixed reference dates: "next Friday" from a Wednesday reference resolves to the Friday of the following week or the coming Friday per the pinned tie-break (the test file documents the chosen semantics); "this Friday", bare "Friday", "March 3" (year omitted, future-resolved), and an explicit past date (rejected) each have a direct test; zero LLM involvement.
2. Parse-service tests (fake gateway): "block next Friday" yields a proposal whose preview carries the resolved concrete date; a model response containing a resolved date instead of tokens is rejected as a schema violation.
3. UI test: the preview renders the concrete resolved date and creation fires only on explicit confirm.
4. The v1 covered-types pinning test is updated, not deleted, and all v1 tests still pass.

title: Code a visit — service code, modifiers, units, place of service, ICD-10 diagnoses
description: A clinician has no way to record what service was delivered, or what it was delivered for, in any coded form. Add coded service and diagnosis fields to the visit — enterable at note creation and editable standalone — so an itemised receipt can be assembled from records the practice already holds.
design:
CONTEXT (code-verified against pablo main, 2026-08-17):

- Rates landed 2026-08-15 (ccb1cd6): appointment-type default fees, per-patient
  override, and scheduling_engine/services/rate_resolver.py. Money is integer
  minor units and "unset" is already distinguishable from zero. Read the
  resolved rate; do not re-derive a fee here.
- patient.diagnosis (models/patient.py:25) is a free-text str | None. It is NOT
  a coded diagnosis list and cannot serve one.
- ICD-10 reference data is ALREADY in the repo:
  backend/app/diagnostics/data/icd10cm_2026.tsv. Validate against it rather than
  adding a second copy or calling out to a service.
- No service-code field exists anywhere in the tree, and no visit-code suggester
  exists either — an earlier spec assumed one and was wrong.
- The provider block a receipt needs is already on the user model: npi_number
  (:114), license_number (:107), license_state (:108), business_address (:109).

PROBLEM: a clinician cannot record what service was delivered or what it was
delivered for, in any coded form. That makes an itemised receipt for
out-of-network reimbursement (PABLO-y7u) impossible to assemble, and it is the
single reason that work is stalled.

SCOPE: let a clinician record billing codes on a visit.

WHERE THEY LIVE — on the VISIT (appointment/session), not on the note document.
One visit can carry several notes, and a visit can exist with no note at all, so
the note is the wrong owner. Anything that renders a receipt later must read one
authoritative place.

WHERE THEY ARE ENTERED — two surfaces, one store:
  (a) At note creation. This is the primary surface: the session duration and the
      clinical picture are both on screen, which is the accurate and
      audit-defensible moment to code. Coding a month later from memory is the
      error-prone chore this work exists to remove.
  (b) A standalone edit on the visit, for after-the-fact correction and for
      visits that never get a note.
Both paths write the same record.

FIELDS per visit:
  - service code (CPT), free-entry string
  - up to four modifiers (e.g. 95 telehealth, 93 audio-only)
  - unit count
  - place-of-service code — a closed enum (11 office, 02 telehealth other than
    home, 10 telehealth in home). Payers deny on a missing or wrong value, so it
    is a field, not a rendering-time guess.
  - an ORDERED list of ICD-10 diagnosis codes (order matters — the first is
    primary)

NOTHING INFERS. No code is suggested, defaulted, or derived — from duration, from
note text, or from anything else. Coding is the clinician's professional
judgement and this surface must not influence it. Duration-derived CPT
suggestion is explicitly OUT of this bead; it is a separate change with a
different risk profile.

The free-text patient.diagnosis field stays exactly as it is. This is additive.

FILES: backend/app/models/scheduling.py, backend/app/db/models.py,
backend/app/db/tenant_template.sql, a new alembic revision,
backend/app/routes/scheduling.py, the note-creation route, and the booking +
note-creation frontend surfaces.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A visit can carry a service code, up to four modifiers, a unit count, a
   place-of-service code, and an ordered list of ICD-10 diagnosis codes. All of
   them round-trip through the API, and diagnosis order is preserved.
2. Every field is optional. Existing appointments keep working with all of them
   null, and the migration adds no NOT NULL column without a default.
3. An ICD-10 code absent from backend/app/diagnostics/data/icd10cm_2026.tsv is
   rejected with a clear message naming the offending code; a code present in it
   is accepted. Tests cover both.
4. Place of service is a closed enum. An unknown value is rejected, not stored.
5. Codes are settable from the note-creation flow and from a standalone edit on
   the visit, and both write the same record. A test asserts the two paths
   converge on one stored value.
6. Nothing infers or defaults a code. A test asserts that creating a visit, and
   creating a note on a visit, both leave the codes unset rather than populated.
7. "Unset" stays distinguishable from empty everywhere the codes surface — an
   uncoded visit must not render as a blank code.
8. An Alembic revision ships in the same commit as the model change, upgrades
   cleanly from the current head, and tenant_template.sql is regenerated.
9. Lint, format and type checks pass, and the existing test suite stays green.

title: Record what kind of operator a practice serves, defaulting to clinical
description:
Everything downstream assumes a practice is clinical — patients, appointments, notes, charts. A deployment serving a non-clinical operator has none of those, and there is currently no way to declare that, so surfaces would have to infer it from which tables are empty.

Adds an edition column to the practice record defaulting to the clinical case, so the fact is declared rather than guessed. No behaviour branches on it in this change.
design:
Code-verified 2026-08-11.

`PracticeRow` (`backend/app/db/platform_models.py:42`, platform schema) records
what a practice IS, but not what KIND of operator it serves. Everything
downstream currently assumes a clinical practice: patients, appointments,
notes, charts. A deployment serving a non-clinical operator has none of those,
and today there is no way to say so.

Add an `edition` column recording the kind of operator, so surfaces can branch
on a declared fact instead of inferring one from which tables happen to be
empty.

## Values

- `therapist` — a clinical practice. THE DEFAULT, so every existing row and
  every new row is unchanged in behaviour.
- `personal` — a non-clinical operator. No patients, no charts, no clinical
  severity floors.

## String + CHECK, not a native enum

Follow the column style this table already uses (`is_pentest`,
`audio_retention_days` are both plain columns with DB-level CHECK
constraints). A native Postgres enum type requires `ALTER TYPE` to gain a
value; a CHECK constraint is a plain constraint swap. Editions are expected to
grow, so the cheaper-to-change form wins. Python-side it is still a proper
enum/Literal — the looseness is only in the storage type.

`NOT NULL` with `server_default='therapist'` so the migration needs no
backfill pass and no window where the column is null.

## Deliberately NOT in this change

- No behaviour branches on the value yet. This lands the fact; consumers adopt
  it separately. A migration that also rewires six read paths is unreviewable
  and un-revertable.
- No API for changing it. Editions are set at provisioning time; a
  self-service switch is a different question with data-migration
  consequences (a practice with patients cannot simply become non-clinical).
- No new enum for anything else. `product` already exists on this table, only
  ever holds `"pablo"`, and is not the same axis — leave it alone rather than
  overloading it.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `practices` gains an `edition` column, NOT NULL, server default
   `'therapist'`, constrained at the DB level to the allowed values.
2. An Alembic revision ships in the same commit and upgrades cleanly from the
   current head. Every pre-existing row reads `therapist` afterwards with no
   backfill step.
3. The constraint rejects an unknown value at the database level. A test
   asserts the insert fails rather than silently storing it.
4. The Python-side type is a proper enum/Literal, not a bare string, and is
   exported for consumers.
5. No existing read path changes behaviour. The full test suite passes
   unchanged, and a test asserts a default-edition practice behaves exactly as
   before.
6. Downgrade drops the column and the constraint cleanly.
7. `product` is untouched.
8. Lint, format, and type checks pass.

title: Superbill: deterministic itemised receipt for out-of-network reimbursement
description:
Patients seeing an out-of-network clinician submit an itemised receipt to their own insurer to get reimbursed. Producing one by hand each month is a recurring, error-prone chore, and an error costs the patient a denied claim.

Generates the document deterministically from records the practice already holds. No claim submission and no clearinghouse — the patient files, not the practice.
design:
Code-verified 2026-08-11 against the repo.

A superbill is an itemised receipt the patient submits to their own insurer for
out-of-network reimbursement. The practice never files anything; the document
is generated, handed to the patient, and that is the end of the workflow. This
is deliberately NOT claim submission — no 837, no clearinghouse, no eligibility
check, no accounts-receivable tracking. Those are a different product.

## Composition

Fixed-format PDF, entirely deterministic. **No language model anywhere in this
path** — every field is copied from a record or computed arithmetically. A
reimbursement document that paraphrases is a document that can be wrong in a
way nobody catches until the patient's claim is denied.

- **Provider block** — name, NPI, license. `npi_number` already exists on the
  user model (`backend/app/models/user.py:114`, validated to 10 digits); read
  it rather than adding a second home for the same fact. A missing NPI must
  block generation with a clear message, not render an empty line: a superbill
  without an NPI is not reimbursable and issuing one wastes the patient's time.
- **Patient block** — name, date of birth, address as recorded.
- **Per-visit lines** — date of service, CPT/service code, ICD-10 diagnosis,
  fee, amount paid. Fee resolves through the rates work rather than being
  entered twice.
- **Totals** — sum of fees and sum of payments, computed from the lines shown.
  The document must never total anything it does not also itemise.

## Codes

Service and diagnosis codes are entered or confirmed by the clinician. Nothing
in this path infers, suggests, or defaults a diagnosis code — coding is the
clinician's professional judgement and a receipt is the wrong surface to
influence it.

## Boundaries

Generation is on demand for a chosen patient and date range. Rendering happens
server-side; the PDF is streamed to the caller and not persisted as a new
document type in this piece of work.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Generating a superbill for a patient and date range returns a PDF
   containing the provider block, patient block, one line per visit in range,
   and totals.
2. No language-model call occurs anywhere in the generation path. A test
   asserts this.
3. Generation with a missing provider NPI fails with an explicit error naming
   the missing field, and produces no PDF.
4. Per-visit lines carry date of service, service code, diagnosis code, fee,
   and amount paid. A visit missing a required code is reported, not silently
   omitted from the document.
5. Totals equal the sum of the lines rendered. A test with a date range that
   excludes some visits proves the totals move with the lines.
6. The same inputs produce a byte-identical document across runs, apart from
   any generation timestamp. A test asserts determinism.
7. No diagnosis or service code is inferred, suggested, or defaulted anywhere
   in the path.
8. The fee shown comes from the resolved session rate rather than a second
   independent source.
9. Lint, format, and type checks pass, and the existing test suite stays green.

title: Session rates: appointment-type defaults, per-patient override, sliding-scale note
description:
Clinicians charge different amounts for different appointment types, and reduced-fee arrangements are per-person. Today neither is recorded anywhere, so any statement or receipt has to be assembled by hand.

Adds a practice-level default fee per appointment type, an optional per-patient rate override, and a free-text sliding-scale note, plus one resolver that expresses the precedence between them.
design:
Code-verified 2026-08-11 against the repo.

Two independent places a rate can come from, resolved in a fixed order.

1. **Appointment-type defaults** — a practice-level default fee per appointment
   type, edited in practice settings. This is the common case: most clinicians
   charge one number for a standard session and another for an intake.
2. **Per-patient override** — a rate on the patient record that wins over the
   type default when set. Reduced-fee and sliding-scale arrangements are
   per-person by nature, so this must be a real column and not a note someone
   has to remember to read.
3. **Sliding-scale note** — free text on the patient record recording the
   arrangement in the clinician's own words (e.g. "reduced through June,
   revisit at intake anniversary"). Never parsed, never used in arithmetic;
   it exists so the reason survives staff turnover and the clinician's memory.

Resolution order is patient override -> appointment-type default -> unset.
"Unset" is a legitimate state and must not silently become zero: a statement
line with a blank fee is a visible prompt to fill it in, while a zero is a
wrong number that looks deliberate.

Fees are stored as integer minor units (cents), never floats. Currency is a
single practice-level setting; do not thread a currency per row until there is
a second one to thread.

Schema lives alongside the existing patient and scheduling models
(`backend/app/models/patient.py`, `backend/app/models/scheduling.py`), with an
Alembic revision in `backend/alembic/versions/` in the same style as its
neighbours. Anything that later renders money — statements, receipts — reads
the resolved rate rather than re-deriving the precedence rules itself, so the
order above has exactly one implementation.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A practice can set a default fee per appointment type, and the value
   round-trips through the API.
2. A patient can carry a rate override plus a free-text sliding-scale note;
   both are optional and both round-trip.
3. A single resolver returns the effective rate for (patient, appointment
   type) using patient override -> type default -> unset, and it is the only
   place that precedence is expressed. A test covers all three outcomes.
4. "Unset" is distinguishable from zero everywhere it surfaces. A test asserts
   an unresolved rate does not render as 0.
5. Fees are stored and returned as integer minor units; no float arithmetic
   appears in the rate path.
6. An Alembic revision ships in the same commit as the model change and
   upgrades cleanly from the current head.
7. Existing patients and appointment types keep working with every rate field
   null — the migration adds no NOT NULL column without a default.
8. Lint, format, and type checks pass, and the existing test suite stays green.

description:
There is no test anywhere that exercises POST /api/appointments. Two behavioral

written down first as executable assertions.

including the three known holes, so the next changes flip assertions instead of

change to pass, the test is wrong for this bead - assert the current (wrong)
behavior and mark it.

already used in backend/tests/test_availability_engine.py.

title: Make the scheduling engine authoritative: cover the write path, enforce what it evaluates, and give the read path a consumer
description:
The availability engine is well tested and almost unused. It evaluates all
eight rule types correctly with 34 passing tests, but it is wired into two
read-only routes that nothing calls, and the appointment write path never
consults it at all. A booking at 3am on a blocked day returns 201, and two
appointments at the same time both succeed.

This epic gives the engine arteries and teeth: characterize the write path as
it behaves today, then make it refuse what is physically impossible, then make
it honour the rules it already evaluates, and finally give the read path a real
consumer in the scheduling UI.
design:
SEQUENCE MATTERS. Characterization tests land first so the two behavioral
changes flip existing assertions rather than authoring them from scratch -
there is currently NO test anywhere that calls POST /api/appointments.

  1. Characterize the write path (start node).
  2. Refuse double-booking - collisions are physics.
  3. Enforce availability rules - HARD refuses, SOFT warns. Rules are policy.
  4. Distinguish "not configured" from "no openings" so callers can tell them
     apart, and keep the write path permissive when nothing is configured.
  5. Give the read path a consumer: a "find a time" affordance in the
     appointment flow, the first caller of the free-slots route.

PERMISSIVE WHEN UNCONFIGURED is load-bearing throughout: most practices have
no rules today, and enforcement must not break their booking.

KEY PATHS:
  backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py  (engine)
  backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py:42 (write path)
  backend/app/routes/scheduling.py:193                    (create route)
  backend/tests/test_availability_engine.py               (34 tests to mirror)

title: Consolidate 5 pending changes to backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py
design:
FILED BY THE ENG HEAD, NOT BY A HUMAN. 5 open changes all
conflict on the same file. Each was specified independently and each is
individually reasonable; together they are one piece of work, and landing them
one at a time costs 5 rebase-and-resolve cycles that each re-derive the
same integration.

TARGET FILE: backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py

SOURCE CHANGES:
  - PABLO-o42 (PR #641, branch work/skip-refuted-checks): feat(pentest): add a persistent hypothesis ledger across runs
  - PABLO-ct2 (PR #642, branch work/report-cli-endpoint-bypass): Confirm the managed LLM endpoint before the pentest narrative call
  - PABLO-c2u (PR #643, branch work/narrative-gen-fallback): Fall back to the alternate LLM CLI before giving up on the narrative
  - PABLO-dns (PR #644, branch work/vary-retry-param): Vary sampling and escalate to an alternate model on pentest narrative retries
  - PABLO-o5m (PR #646, branch work/cross-tenant-probe): Run the cross-tenant IDOR probe as a deterministic collector

WHAT TO BUILD. One branch and one PR that satisfies EVERY acceptance block
below. Read all 5 source designs first — they are reproduced in full at the
end — and look for the shared structure before writing anything. Where the file
resists all of them for the same reason, fix that reason; a consolidation whose
only content is 5 changes stacked in one diff has done the mechanical half and
skipped the valuable half.

WHAT NOT TO DO:
  - Do NOT start from any of the existing branches. This is a new branch off
    main. The existing PRs stay open and untouched; they are closed by a human
    once this lands, and reading them is allowed but inheriting them is not.
  - Do NOT drop, defer, or "simplify away" any acceptance block. If one of them
    genuinely cannot coexist with another, that is a real finding: STOP, print
    WORKER-BLOCKED with the two blocks and why they conflict, and open no PR.
    A conflict between two specs is a decision for a human, not a tiebreak for
    a worker.
  - Do NOT change behaviour the acceptance blocks do not ask you to change. The
    existing test suite for this file is the invariant: every test that passed
    before must pass after.

HOW THIS IS CHECKED. A separate reviewer, which sees ONLY the final diff and the
acceptance blocks — not this design, not your commits, not your reasoning — will
answer each block with satisfied / not satisfied / cannot tell. Anything other
than satisfied blocks the merge and names the block that went missing. Write the
diff so that a reader with no context can find each block satisfied in it.

SOURCE DESIGNS, IN FULL:

--- PABLO-o42: feat(pentest): add a persistent hypothesis ledger across runs ---
Store alongside the evidence bundle and persist to the same reports bucket so the ledger survives between runs; read the last N (start with 8) at prompt-build time. Record the chain sketch in the same anchored form the design doc already requires — expressible as a sequence of HTTP requests, SQL queries or cloud API calls against the deployed system — so an entry is checkable rather than a vibe. Out of scope: acting on ledger entries automatically, and any change to how findings are reported.

--- PABLO-ct2: Confirm the managed LLM endpoint before the pentest narrative call ---
Make the routing explicit rather than incidental. Options in preference order: (1) assert it — before invoking, resolve which endpoint the CLI will use and fail closed if it is not the managed one; (2) record it — write the resolved endpoint and auth mode into the report's attestation block so every archived report states where the text came from; (3) remove the ambiguity — call the managed endpoint directly for the narrative step instead of shelling out to a CLI whose auth precedence is not ours to control. (3) composes well with splitting deterministic synthesis from agentic exploration. Touch points: _invoke_gemini / _invoke_claude / _run_cli (~541-590), the attestation block in _assemble_report.

--- PABLO-c2u: Fall back to the alternate LLM CLI before giving up on the narrative ---
Touch points: backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py — _invoke_llm (~line 410), the retry wrapper at ~466-500, the NARRATIVE GENERATION FAILED block at ~520, and run()/sys.exit at ~777. _MIN_NARRATIVE_CHARS (3000) stays the heuristic. Keep the existing narrative-failed report block verbatim; this bead changes control flow and exit status only. Out of scope: changing the prompt text (tracked on the collector bead), changing the format-failure threshold, provisioning the alternate model's entitlement.

--- PABLO-dns: Vary sampling and escalate to an alternate model on pentest narrative retries ---
Touch points: _invoke_llm (~410), the retry wrapper (~466-500), _invoke_gemini / _invoke_claude (~541-572). The gemini CLI takes generation settings via its own flags/config — check what 0.38.x exposes before assuming temperature is reachable; if it is not, escalate straight to the model/provider ladder. Keep _MIN_NARRATIVE_CHARS as the failure heuristic. Order: attempt 1 default -> attempt 2 reinforced + varied sampling -> attempt 3 alternate model -> fail. Composes with PABLO-c2u (nonzero exit + alternate chaining); land that first if they are worked separately.

--- PABLO-o5m: Run the cross-tenant IDOR probe as a deterministic collector ---
Touch points: backend/app/jobs/pentest_collectors.py (new collector, mirror the shape of the existing collectors and their bundle-summary entries), backend/app/jobs/pentest_runner.py::_build_prompt STEP 4 and STEP 5 (lines ~370-395). The two ephemeral identities are already provisioned by backend/app/jobs/pentest_identity.py and reach the prompt as PENTEST_TEST_ID_TOKEN_A/B, PENTEST_TEST_EMAIL_A/B, PENTEST_TEST_UID_A/B — the collector reads the same values. Severity classification for a FAIL stays where it already lives (backend/app/jobs/pentest_severity.py); the collector reports the observation, not the tier. Out of scope: adding new probe classes (intra-tenant IDOR is tracked separately), changing which scanners run, any IAM or infrastructure change.
acceptance_criteria:
Every block below must be satisfied by the single resulting diff. They are reproduced verbatim from the 5 source beads; they are numbered so the reviewer can answer each one separately.

[1] FROM PABLO-o42 — feat(pentest): add a persistent hypothesis ledger across runs
- Each run appends one ledger record per hypothesis considered, with outcome.
- The prompt receives the last N runs of ledger entries.
- A run that re-proposes a previously REFUTED chain must state what changed; a test asserts the instruction is present and that the ledger is fed forward.
- The ledger persists between runs and is readable independently of any single report.
- Unit tests cover: append, read-last-N, empty-ledger first run.
- make check passes.

[2] FROM PABLO-ct2 — Confirm the managed LLM endpoint before the pentest narrative call
- Every generated report states, in the attestation block, which endpoint and auth mode produced the narrative.
- A run that cannot confirm the managed endpoint fails rather than proceeding.
- A unit test covers the fail-closed path.
- make check passes.

[3] FROM PABLO-c2u — Fall back to the alternate LLM CLI before giving up on the narrative
- When the primary model fails the format-failure heuristic on both the initial
  and reinforced attempts, the runner invokes the alternate CLI once before
  giving up.

title: [bug] test_update_status_to_discontinued_sets_stopped_at fails on any branch between 8pm and midnight US Eastern
design:
FOUND 2026-08-02 22:58 ET while running an unrelated frontend-only change
through `make check`.

backend/tests/test_routes_medications.py:224 compares a stopped_at value the
server derives in UTC against a locally computed date.today(). Between 20:00 and
23:59 US Eastern the UTC calendar date has already rolled over to tomorrow while
the local date has not, so the two disagree and the test fails. It passes at
every other hour, on every branch, with no code change involved.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY FLAKE. It is not random - it is a
deterministic function of wall-clock time, so it cannot be reproduced by
re-running in the morning and looks like "the branch broke it" to whoever hits
it. And `make check` is a stated acceptance criterion on a large number of
beads, so during that four-hour window EVERY such bead has an unsatisfiable
acceptance criterion. An automated worker that hits it has no way to know the
failure is pre-existing and unrelated: it either burns its remaining budget
investigating backend code it never touched, or it declines to push work that
was actually complete. Both look like worker failure and neither is.

FIX: make the assertion timezone-honest rather than time-of-day dependent -
compare against the same UTC-derived date the server used (or freeze time).
Do not "fix" it by widening the assertion to accept either date; that hides
a real timezone bug class if one ever appears.

WORTH A SWEEP: this is unlikely to be the only test comparing a server UTC
value to a local date.today() / datetime.now(). Grep the suite for naive
date.today() and datetime.now() in assertions while you are in here.
acceptance_criteria:
- The test passes at any hour. Prove it by running the suite with the clock
  (or TZ) set into the 20:00-23:59 US Eastern window, not just by re-running it
  at a convenient time.
- Any sibling assertions comparing a server-side UTC value against a naive local
  date/time are found and fixed or explicitly ruled out.
- `make check` passes at the repo root.

title: Enforce availability rules on the appointment write path — HARD refuses, SOFT warns
design:
AVAILABILITY RULES ARE ADVISORY. The engine evaluates all eight rule types
correctly and has 34 passing tests, but it is wired into TWO read-only routes
and nothing else. A booking at 3am on a blocked day returns 201.

PROVEN 2026-08-02:
  - AvailabilityEngine is constructed in one factory
    (backend/app/routes/scheduling.py:150) and injected into exactly two routes,
    both read-only:
        :551  GET  /api/availability/slots
        :568  POST /api/availability/check
  - The write path never touches it: routes/scheduling.py:193 create_appointment
    -> scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py:42, which validates only
    patient_id / start_at / end_at / duration_minutes.
  - EnforcementLevel (HARD | SOFT) is defined at
    scheduling_engine/models/availability.py:24 and READ in exactly one
    expression in production code: routes/scheduling.py:584,
    `has_hard = any(c.enforcement == EnforcementLevel.HARD ...)`, which only
    shapes the response body of the check route. Nothing acts on it. The engine
    itself never inspects enforcement - it copies it onto the Conflict and moves
    on.
  - No frontend code calls /api/availability/* at all. The read path has no
    consumer today.

THE TELL: a two-level enforcement enum that no code enforces is a design that
anticipated a step nobody built. HARD vs SOFT is meaningless until something
refuses.

DEPENDS ON the double-booking bead. Both change the same functions
(create_appointment / update_appointment); landing them in parallel guarantees a
conflict. Collisions first (physics), then rules (policy).

SCOPE:
  1. Give SchedulingService access to AvailabilityEngine. The engine's
     constructor already takes (rule_repo, appointment_repo)
     - services/availability.py:40 - and the factory at routes/scheduling.py:150
     shows the DI shape. Keep SchedulingService constructible with just the repo
     so the ~35 existing tests that do SchedulingService(repo) keep compiling:
     an optional availability_engine parameter defaulting to None, with rule
     checking skipped when it is absent.
  2. On create, and on update when a time field changes, call
     engine.check_conflicts(user_id, start_at, end_at) - signature at
     services/availability.py:48, returns list[Conflict].
  3. Partition the result by conflict.enforcement:
       HARD -> refuse. Raise a rule-violation error mapped to HTTP 422, with
               every violated rule's message in the body. 422 distinguishes
               "you may not book this" from the 409 the collision bead returns
               for "something is already there" - two different fixes for the
               user, so two different codes.
       SOFT -> allow, and return the warnings alongside the created
               appointment so the caller can surface them. A SOFT rule that
               silently vanishes is the same bug in a smaller box.
  4. Identity: the write routes use user.id (from require_baa_acceptance) while
     the availability routes use ctx.user_id (TenantContext). Same value in
     practice today. Pick one deliberately and be consistent - the engine's
     methods are written against ctx.user_id.

KNOWN SHARP EDGES, worth handling or explicitly deferring in the notes:
  - rule.params is an untyped dict with NO validation at any layer
    (models/availability.py:40); the create-rule route passes it through raw
    (:631). Malformed params surface as a KeyError from inside the engine
    (e.g. availability.py:154). Once rules gate writes, a bad rule stops being a
    cosmetic problem and starts refusing legitimate bookings. Either validate
    params per rule type, or catch and treat an unevaluable rule as
    non-blocking - do NOT let a KeyError become a 500 on the booking path.
  - Buffer minutes are wall-clock and same-day clamped
    (availability.py:375-391), so an appointment crossing midnight is silently
    truncated. Note it; fixing it is not this bead.

OUT OF SCOPE: overlap detection (the dependency owns it), UI, and any
per-clinician policy table.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A booking that violates a HARD rule (blocked day, outside working hours) is
   refused with 422 and a body naming the violated rule; the appointment is not
   created.
2. A booking that violates only a SOFT rule succeeds and returns the warnings.
3. A booking that violates nothing still succeeds.
4. A user with no rules is unaffected.
5. The same enforcement applies to PATCH when a time field changes, and the
   start-session internal update still does not trip it.
6. A malformed rule (params missing an expected key) does not 500 the booking
   path - covered by a test.
7. Tests call POST /api/appointments through the route, not just the service.
8. `make check` passes at the repo root.
notes:
Paths verified present on main 2026-08-16: backend/app/routes/scheduling.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/models/availability.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/scheduling.py, backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py.

Sequencing note: this and the double-booking refusal both edit the scheduling route and service. They are complementary, not duplicates — one enforces the therapist's availability rules, the other rejects overlaps — but they touch the same two files, so they must not be worked simultaneously. Whichever starts first should land before the other begins; the second will need to rebase on it.

title: Add an overlap query to the appointment repository — list_overlapping on the ABC and both implementations
design:
THE MISSING PRIMITIVE. Nothing in the appointment repository can answer "does
this proposed time collide with an existing appointment?", which is why the
write path cannot check for double-booking even though it obviously should.
This bead adds ONLY that primitive plus its tests. No route changes, no service
changes - those follow in a separate bead so this one lands small and green.

WHY list_by_range IS NOT IT (verified 2026-08-02):
  backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment.py:85-87 filters
      AppointmentRow.user_id == user_id
      AppointmentRow.start_at >= start
      AppointmentRow.start_at <  end
  It selects on start_at ONLY. An appointment that begins before the window and
  ends inside it is not returned. The in-memory implementation has the identical
  semantic (backend/app/scheduling_engine/repositories/appointment.py:161). Using
  it for collision detection silently misses every long appointment that spans
  the proposed start - the exact case a therapist hits with a 90-minute intake.

CORRECT OVERLAP PREDICATE (half-open intervals, so back-to-back appointments do
NOT collide):
      existing.start_at <  proposed_end
  AND existing.end_at   >  proposed_start

ADD TO THE ABC - backend/app/scheduling_engine/repositories/appointment.py:17,
alongside list_by_range (:25):

    @abstractmethod
    def list_overlapping(
        self,
        user_id: str,
        start: str | datetime,
        end: str | datetime,
        *,
        exclude_appointment_id: str | None = None,
    ) -> list[Appointment]:
        ...

  - user_id is the calendar-ownership slice, matching list_by_range and the
    availability engine (see the authorization note at
    backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment.py:39-52). Do NOT route this
    through the patient_clinicians authorization path - collision detection is
    about one clinician's calendar.
  - exclude_appointment_id exists so a reschedule can ask "would this collide
    with anything OTHER than the appointment I am moving?". Without it, moving
    an appointment by five minutes collides with itself.
  - Cancelled appointments MUST be excluded, in the query, not by the caller.
    Match the existing convention exactly: the codebase compares the bare string
    "cancelled" (backend/app/scheduling_engine/services/availability.py:80, 212,
    242, 267). Be consistent with that rather than introducing a second spelling.

IMPLEMENT IN BOTH:
  - backend/app/repositories/postgres/appointment.py - mirror list_by_range
    (:71) for session handling, row->model mapping and datetime coercion. Only
    the WHERE clause differs.
  - backend/app/scheduling_engine/repositories/appointment.py - the in-memory
    implementation used by every unit test (:161 is the list_by_range twin).
  The two must agree; a divergence here is invisible until production.

OUT OF SCOPE, ON PURPOSE: wiring this into create/update, availability rules,
buffers, and any HTTP surface. This bead ends at "the repository can answer the
question".
acceptance_criteria:
1. list_overlapping is on the AppointmentRepository ABC and implemented in BOTH
   the Postgres and in-memory repositories with identical semantics.
2. Unit tests covering, against BOTH implementations (parametrize or mirror):
   a. Exact same start and end -> collides.
   b. Existing appointment fully contains the proposed slot -> collides.
   c. Proposed slot fully contains an existing appointment -> collides.
   d. Existing starts BEFORE the window and ends inside it -> collides. This is
      the case list_by_range misses; a test that passes with list_by_range's
      predicate has not proven anything.
   e. Back-to-back (existing ends exactly when proposed starts) -> does NOT
      collide.
   f. A cancelled appointment overlapping the slot -> does NOT collide.
   g. exclude_appointment_id omits that appointment from the result.
   h. An appointment belonging to a different user_id -> not returned.
3. `make check` passes at the repo root (lint includes mypy; ruff + pytest alone
   is not sufficient).

title: Split the exploratory pass into generate / execute / classify, driven by personas with motive
description:
Today the exploratory half is one undifferentiated instruction: read the bundle, probe things, write the report. That shape produces a checklist, because generating an idea and testing it compete for the same attention and testing always wins — the model reaches for what it already knows how to run.

Split it into three passes.

GENERATE — no tools. Given the domain-model context pack (PABLO-usn), the hypothesis ledger (PABLO-o42), and a small set of personas, produce a ranked list of hypotheses. Each must be anchored: expressible as a concrete sequence of requests, queries or cloud API calls against the deployed system. Unanchorable ideas are dropped, which is what removes generic filler.

EXECUTE — tools, bounded. Take the top N and attempt them.

CLASSIFY — each attempt resolves to CONFIRMED, REFUTED or PARTIAL, with the observed evidence, and every outcome is written to the ledger.

Personas beat actor labels because a persona forces a completed narrative — an incentive and a constraint — rather than a classification. 'Authenticated user, cross-boundary' is a category; 'an administrator whose access was revoked an hour ago and who wants one more export' is a story that names its own chain steps, and it lands directly on the token-revocation-lag gap the coverage doc already records. Start with three: a curious practitioner poking at a colleague's records inside their own practice, a recently-offboarded administrator, and a party fishing for records they have no lawful claim to.
design: Three separate model invocations, not three sections of one prompt — the separation is the mechanism. GENERATE runs without tool access so it cannot shortcut into executing the first idea. Bound EXECUTE by count and wall clock, and log every tool invocation. CLASSIFY writes to the ledger regardless of outcome, including UNTESTED for hypotheses that ran out of budget, so the next run knows what was left rather than silently re-proposing it. Personas belong in configuration, not hard-coded, so the set can grow without a code change. Out of scope: the deployment target and rules of engagement (tracked separately), and any change to the deterministic checks.
acceptance_criteria:
- Generation, execution and classification are three separate invocations; generation has no tool access.
- Every hypothesis is anchored to a concrete request/query sequence, and unanchorable ones are dropped with a recorded reason.
- Every hypothesis resolves to CONFIRMED / REFUTED / PARTIAL / UNTESTED and is written to the ledger.
- Personas are configuration, not code, and at least three ship with distinct motives.
- Execution is bounded by both count and wall clock, and exceeding either is recorded rather than silent.
- Unit tests cover: unanchored hypothesis dropped, budget exhausted marks UNTESTED, classification written to ledger.
- make check passes.

title: Build a domain-model context pack for the assessment prompt instead of generic security framing
description:
The exploratory half of the assessment is fed category framing, which crowds out the thing that actually produces non-obvious hypotheses: this system's own authorization model.

Concrete example of what is being missed. This application has TWO authorization boundaries — schema-level isolation between practices, and the per-patient clinician grant path (patient_clinicians / has_patient_access, enforced across medications, patient documents and the patient repositories). A model told only 'check for broken access control' will test the first and never consider the second. A model handed both boundaries as facts can ask whether the grant path itself is forgeable through mass assignment on an update endpoint — a specific, testable, non-obvious question that generic framing will never reach.

Assemble the facts the system already collects into a structured context pack and give the exploration prompt that instead: the route table with its auth dependencies annotated, the RLS policy and schema inventory already gathered by the Cloud SQL collector, the grant-table enforcement points, and the egress/subprocessor manifest.
design: Build the pack from existing collector output wherever possible rather than new collection — the Cloud SQL collector already gathers policies and the schema list, and the route table is derivable from the app's own router registration. Keep it structured (not prose) so it is diffable between runs and cheap in context. Pair it with the anchoring constraint the design doc already specifies: a hypothesis that cannot be expressed as concrete requests against the deployed system is omitted. Replace generic category lists rather than adding to them — context budget spent on a checklist is context not spent on the domain. Out of scope: new collectors, changing the deterministic checks.
acceptance_criteria:
- A structured context pack is assembled from existing collector output and passed to the exploration prompt.
- Generic security-category framing is removed from that prompt, not merely supplemented.
- The pack includes both authorization boundaries — schema isolation and the per-patient grant path — as explicit facts.
- A test asserts the pack contains the grant-path facts and that the prompt no longer carries the category list.
- make check passes.
